results.title: France Fridge Cyberattacks: Paris links Iran IRGC to supermarket sabotage, weighs retaliation against Tehran
results.description: France has accused Iran of orchestrating a series of cyberattacks that sabotaged supermarket refrigeration systems across the country, with Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot warning that Paris is considering retaliatory measures, including sanctions and travel restrictions. The French government summoned Iran’s ambassador on November 10 after an investigation attributed the cyberattacks to Shahid Kaveh, an affiliate of the cyber unit of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Barrot said France was “not ruling anything out” in its response, signalling that diplomatic and economic measures remain under consideration. Speaking to Franceinfo radio, Barrot said possible measures included prohibiting individuals held responsible from entering European territory and freezing their assets. Paris is also preparing to propose new European sanctions against Iranian individuals and entities allegedly involved in the sabotage operation. The cyberattacks targeted approximately 700 grocery stores during the night of 11–12 October, remotely manipulating refrigeration systems and causing temperatures inside refrigerators and freezers to rise by as much as 50 degrees Celsius. Investigation traces attacks to Iranian-linked cyber unit According to the findings presented by French authorities, the operation affected major supermarket chains, including Intermarche, E. Leclerc, Carrefour, Monoprix and Cooperative U. The disruption caused food spoilage, fires and damage estimated at tens of millions of dollars. Investigators identified the use of Farsi and internet protocol addresses pointing to devices in Iran. The Paris Prosecutor’s Office said the cyberattacks were carried out in the interests of a foreign power, identified as Iran. Read More: From Non-Alignment to Multi-Alignment: How India is emerging as a key power in the new world order The attackers reportedly gained remote access to refrigeration controllers supplied by Danish engineering company Danfoss and Italian manufacturer Dixell. Using web interfaces, they took control of the equipment, initiated continuous defrost cycles and disabled safety alerts designed to warn operators when temperatures crossed critical thresholds. The manipulation caused refrigeration units to heat up, compromising food storage and triggering fires in some locations. Paris chief prosecutor Laure Beccuau said investigators were seeking international arrest warrants in connection with the operation. France’s Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs described the incident as an unprecedented cyber campaign in terms of its scale and aggressiveness. It characterised the operation as the first cyber offensive against French territory conducted purely for sabotage. The ministry said the attacks threatened critical infrastructure, violated international law and could not be justified. Tehran rejects accusations as European attacks widen Iran rejected the cyberattack allegations on 10 November, describing them as baseless and malicious. In a statement, its Foreign Ministry accused France of making repeated allegations to divert attention from its policies towards Iran and West Asia. Tehran said the accusations were intended to damage its international image and relations with other countries. France has previously attributed cyber operations and information manipulation campaigns against the country to Iranian-linked actors. These include attacks targeting the satirical publication Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and the Paris Olympics in 2024. The allegations led to European sanctions in March 2026 against Iranian private company Emennet Pasargad. The supermarket attacks have also raised concerns beyond France. During November, retailers in Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Finland, Ireland and Sweden reported losses after similar refrigeration systems were targeted. French blood banks were also affected by cyberattacks on November 2. The French Blood Establishment said temperature and defrost settings in cold-storage units used for blood products and samples had been altered to excessively high levels. The incidents have added to European concerns over attacks on essential services and critical infrastructure. Separately, a wave of hoax bomb threats has disrupted passenger flights across the region, with several aircraft making emergency landings. France’s response is now likely to involve diplomatic action and efforts to secure wider European measures against those identified by investigators. Barrot’s warning that Paris is not ruling anything out leaves the possibility of further action against Tehran open.
